outcome: No result addressing the infinitude of Leinster groups was found in the window; the only related development is a 2025 paper introducing relaxed variants (almost/quasi-Leinster groups) that explicitly does not tackle the original question.
summary: A Leinster group is a finite group whose order equals the sum of the orders of its normal subgroups (a group-theoretic analogue of perfect numbers). Whether infinitely many exist is stated as open both by the current Wikipedia article ('It is unknown whether there are infinitely many Leinster groups', with no citation or date suggesting recent movement) and by every source found in this search. The only paper from the window (26 Jan 2024 to present) that discusses Leinster groups at all is Pleșca and Tărnăuceanu, 'Almost and quasi Leinster groups' (arXiv:2503.16884, submitted 8 April 2025). That paper deliberately studies relaxed variants — 'almost Leinster' and 'quasi-Leinster' groups, paralleling almost-perfect and quasi-perfect numbers — rather than the original Leinster-group condition. Per §3.1 this is a related/variant problem, not a case of the stated problem: settling questions about almost/quasi-Leinster groups removes nothing from the original infinitude question, since those are different (relaxed) defining equations, not restrictions of the same one. The paper does use GAP (a computer-algebra system, not an AI system) for verification of examples; this is unrelated to AI involvement in any event, and it does not bear on the original problem regardless. No arXiv, Wikipedia, or general-web search surfaced any 2024–2026 work constructing an infinite family of genuine Leinster groups, proving finiteness, or otherwise moving the original question. I also checked the 2019 'Leinster groups of order pqrs' line of work (Zhang/Tărnăuceanu-adjacent classification results) for any recent continuation; searches found only the pre-window (2019) paper and no update in the window. I am satisfied this is a genuine 'nothing happened' case: the problem is a fairly obscure, narrow group-theory question with only a handful of active researchers (chiefly Tărnăuceanu and coauthors), its own Wikipedia article was checked directly and shows no updated claim, and multiple query angles (direct infinitude question, arXiv author search, general open-problem-list search, disambiguation page) converged on the same single 2025 tangential paper.
competing_reading: One could argue the almost/quasi-Leinster paper is indirectly relevant groundwork — e.g. if quasi-Leinster groups were shown to be infinite in a way that structurally suggested a route to infinitely many genuine Leinster groups. But the paper's own framing treats these as distinct, parallel objects (analogous to how almost-perfect numbers are a separate open topic from perfect numbers), and it reports no implication for the genuine case. I do not think this rises to 'partial progress' under §3.1's case-vs-variant test, since it changes the defining equation rather than restricting the class of groups considered under the original equation.
what_would_settle_it: A paper either exhibiting an infinite family of groups satisfying the exact Leinster condition (order = sum of orders of normal subgroups), or a proof that only finitely many such groups exist, or an expert (e.g. Tărnăuceanu, who works actively in this exact niche) explicitly commenting that the question remains open as of a recent date.
